---
title: "How much of Philadelphia's campus poverty is students?"
subtitle: "On the city's poverty map, the blocks around Penn, Drexel and Temple look as poor as anywhere. A third or more of that is students. The rest is not."
author: "Kyle Tong"
date: 2026-10-18
categories:
  - GIS
  - poverty
  - Philadelphia
description: "Splitting tract poverty rates into college students and everyone else shows that Philadelphia's campus neighborhoods are poorer than the city, just not as poor as the map says."
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(here)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

DERIVED <- here("blog", "posts", "post5", "data", "derived")

tracts <- st_read(file.path(DERIVED, "phl_tracts.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)
pooled <- read_csv(file.path(DERIVED, "pooled_rates.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

campus_tracts <- filter(tracts, !is.na(campus_area))

labels <- tibble(label = c("University City", "Temple"),
                 lon = c(-75.212, -75.128), lat = c(39.946, 39.986)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

# Window for the zoomed comparison: both campuses plus about 2.5 km around.
zoom <- st_bbox(st_buffer(st_union(campus_tracts), 2500))

p   <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d)
grp <- function(g, v) pooled[[v]][pooled$group == g]

POV_LIMITS <- c(0, max(c(tracts$pov_all, tracts$pov_noncol), na.rm = TRUE))

tract_map <- function(var, fill_name, scale) {
  ggplot(tracts) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data[[var]]), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
    geom_sf(data = campus_tracts, fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.45) +
    geom_sf_label(data = labels, aes(label = label), size = 3,
                  fontface = "bold", fill = "white", label.size = 0) +
    scale +
    labs(fill = fill_name, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_void(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "right")
}

pov_scale <- scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "rocket", direction = -1,
                                  limits = POV_LIMITS, labels = percent,
                                  na.value = "grey85")
```

A poverty map of Philadelphia shows the neighborhoods around its three big universities in
the same dark shade as Kensington and North Philadelphia. Part of that is real, and part of
it is that college students report very little income.

**The question: how much of the measured poverty around Philadelphia's campuses is college
students, and how poor are these neighborhoods without them?**

The four figures answer this in sequence. @fig-all is the map as usually drawn.
@fig-students shows where off-campus students live. @fig-noncol redraws the first map,
same color scale, with students removed. @fig-dumbbell puts each campus tract's two rates
side by side.

## Data

Census tracts from the 2020-2024 American Community Survey 5-year estimates and Census
TIGER/Line boundaries, both pulled with `tidycensus`. Table B14006 reports poverty status
separately for undergraduates, graduate students and everyone else, so the split is
arithmetic:

```{r}
#| label: split
#| eval: false

pov_all    = pov_poor / pov_universe
pov_noncol = (pov_poor - col_poor) / (pov_universe - col_pop)
```

Poverty status is not measured for people in dormitories, so only off-campus students
enter these numbers. Every map shows rates rather than counts, and tracts with fewer than
500 people in the relevant group are grey. Campus tracts, outlined in black, are tracts
within a kilometre of Penn, Drexel or Temple where students make up at least a quarter of
residents.

## The map as usually drawn

```{r}
#| label: fig-all
#| fig-cap: "Poverty rate, all residents, by census tract. Black outlines mark campus tracts; grey tracts have fewer than 500 residents (parks, the airport, industrial land)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| echo: false

tract_map("pov_all", "poverty rate", pov_scale)
```

Pooled, the campus tracts in University City have a poverty rate of
`r p(grp("University City", "pov_all"))` percent and those around Temple
`r p(grp("Temple", "pov_all"))` percent, against `r p(grp("Rest of city", "pov_all"))`
percent in the rest of the city.

## Where students live

```{r}
#| label: fig-students
#| fig-cap: "Off-campus college and graduate students as a share of residents."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| echo: false

tract_map("student_share", "students",
          scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, labels = percent,
                               na.value = "grey85"))
```

Students cluster in two places, and they are poor on paper:
`r p(grp("University City", "pov_college"), 0)` percent of students in the University City
campus tracts and `r p(grp("Temple", "pov_college"), 0)` percent around Temple fall below
the poverty line, because most live on loans and family support that the survey does not count
as income.

## The same map without students, up close

```{r}
#| label: fig-noncol
#| fig-cap: "Central Philadelphia, poverty rate for all residents (left) and for residents who are not college or graduate students (right). Same color scale as the first map; black outlines mark campus tracts, grey marks tracts with too few residents to measure."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| echo: false

both <- bind_rows(
  mutate(tracts, panel = "all residents", rate = pov_all),
  mutate(tracts, panel = "without students", rate = pov_noncol)
)

ggplot(both) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = rate), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = campus_tracts, fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_sf_label(data = labels, aes(label = label), size = 2.8,
                fontface = "bold", fill = "white", label.size = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  pov_scale +
  coord_sf(xlim = zoom[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = zoom[c("ymin", "ymax")],
           datum = NA) +
  labs(fill = "poverty rate", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11,
                                  margin = margin(b = 4)))
```

Away from the campuses almost nothing changes: the rest of the city goes from
`r p(grp("Rest of city", "pov_all"))` to `r p(grp("Rest of city", "pov_noncol"))` percent.
Around the campuses the dark patches fade without disappearing. Non-student poverty is
`r p(grp("University City", "pov_noncol"))` percent in University City and
`r p(grp("Temple", "pov_noncol"))` percent around Temple.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dumbbell
#| fig-cap: "Each campus tract's poverty rate with and without students. The dashed line is the non-student poverty rate for the rest of the city. Tract 88.01 has too few non-students to measure."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| echo: false

campus_tracts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(pov_noncol)) |>
  mutate(tract = paste0(sub("Census Tract ", "Tract ", NAMELSAD), " (", campus_area, ")"),
         tract = reorder(tract, pov_noncol)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = tract)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = grp("Rest of city", "pov_noncol"),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = pov_noncol, xend = pov_all, yend = tract), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(x = pov_all, colour = "all residents"), size = 2.8) +
  geom_point(aes(x = pov_noncol, colour = "without students"), size = 2.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("all residents" = "#D55E00",
                                 "without students" = "#0072B2"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "poverty rate", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

## What the four figures say together

@fig-all overstates campus poverty, and @fig-students shows why: the dark patches sit
exactly where off-campus students live, and students are almost all poor on paper. But
@fig-noncol shows that removing them does not make the campus neighborhoods ordinary.
Students account for between a third and two fifths of the measured rate, and the
non-students who remain are about half again as likely to be poor as residents of the rest
of the city. Philadelphia's universities sit in poor neighborhoods; the map makes those
neighborhoods look
`r p(grp("University City", "pov_all") / grp("University City", "pov_noncol") - 1, 0)` to
`r p(grp("Temple", "pov_all") / grp("Temple", "pov_noncol") - 1, 0)` percent poorer than
they are.

@fig-dumbbell adds that this is not uniform. Tract 369.02, on the Center City side of
University City, falls to roughly the city average once students are removed, as does
tract 153 near Temple. Tract 147, southwest of Temple's campus, stays above 60 percent.

So both obvious readings of the raw map are wrong. Taking it at face value overstates
poverty near campus; dismissing campus-area poverty as "just students" misses that five of
the seven measurable campus tracts are still above 20 percent without them. For anyone
ranking neighborhoods by need, the correction takes one extra ACS table.

## Caveats

Tract estimates carry wide margins of error, and five-year pooling blends 2020 to 2024,
including the pandemic. The one-kilometre and 25 percent thresholds that define a campus
tract are judgment calls. And "poor on paper" is not the same as hardship for students,
though for their non-student neighbors it usually is.

Scripts are in `R/` and details in `README.md`. Data: U.S. Census Bureau, American
Community Survey 2020-2024 5-year estimates and TIGER/Line cartographic boundary files,
accessed 18 October 2026.
